title: The Interwar Period and Unresolved Tensions
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: The interwar period (1919–1939) was defined by instability. World War I had not resolved the world's tensions but deepened them: the peace was bitter, economies were shattered, and millions lost faith in democracy, capitalism, and the old political order.

In 1923, Germany suffered catastrophic hyperinflation. Prices doubled every few days, a loaf of bread cost hundreds of billions of marks, and a lifetime of savings could be wiped out in a week, illustrating the economic chaos of the early interwar years.

The Treaty of Versailles left a poisonous legacy in Germany, where people resented the 'war guilt' clause, crushing reparations, lost territory, and a gutted military. Germans spoke of being 'stabbed in the back,' and that humiliation became raw material for extremist politicians.

The League of Nations, created to prevent future wars, was fatally weak: the United States never joined, it had no army of its own, and it could only recommend, not enforce. When aggression came, the League proved unable to stop it.

After a fragile 1920s recovery, the U.S. stock market crashed in October 1929. Because the global economy was deeply interconnected, with American loans propping up Europe, the collapse spread worldwide, shrinking trade and closing factories and banks.

At the depths of the Great Depression, unemployment soared to roughly a quarter of American workers and a third of German workers. The crisis discredited the existing capitalist, democratic order and made radical alternatives attractive to desperate people.

Economic catastrophe is political dynamite. Frightened, impoverished, humiliated populations became willing to trade freedom for the promise of bread, order, and national pride, supplying the desperation that fascist and militarist movements fed on.

Totalitarian states sought total control over politics, the economy, culture, information, and even the private beliefs of citizens, typically under a single party and a charismatic leader, enforced by secret police, propaganda, and terror.

Fascism was a radical-right ideology that was ultra-nationalist, glorified the state, nation, and leader above the individual, celebrated military strength and violence, and defined itself fiercely against both democracy and communism.
In Italy, Benito Mussolini exploited postwar chaos and fear of communism to take power in 1922, building the first fascist state and serving as a model for other fascist movements in Europe.

In Germany, Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party rose on Depression-era misery and Versailles resentment, came to power legally in 1933, and then dismantled democracy. Nazism added genocidal racism and antisemitism, blaming Jews for Germany's humiliations and promising conquest of 'living space' (Lebensraum) in the east.

In Japan, the Depression strengthened ultranationalist militarists who increasingly dominated a nominally constitutional government, glorified the emperor and army, and pursued imperial expansion in Asia as the solution to Japan's economic and resource problems.

Born of the Russian Revolution, the USSR under Joseph Stalin became a communist totalitarian state. Stalin forced rapid industrialization through Five-Year Plans, collectivized agriculture (causing famines that killed millions, including in Ukraine), and unleashed the Great Purges.

Fascism and communism were bitter ideological enemies — radical right versus radical left, nationalist versus class-based — yet as forms of government they shared striking features: one-party dictatorship, state control, secret police, propaganda, and the crushing of individual freedom.

Stalin's Great Purges executed or imprisoned millions of supposed enemies of the state, including party members, military officers, and ordinary citizens, using show trials, secret police, and terror to consolidate his totalitarian control.

Hitler's rise illustrates layered causation: long-term Versailles resentment, the immediate economic trigger of the Great Depression (Nazi votes surged as unemployment exploded after 1929), weak democratic institutions, and Hitler's own exploitation of all three combined to bring the Nazis to power.

Germany's fragile democracy could not govern the Depression crisis, and conservative elites handed Hitler the chancellorship in 1933 in the mistaken belief they could control him. Once in power, he quickly outlawed other parties and established a dictatorship.

Strong comparison analysis chooses meaningful categories (ideology, economic policy, methods of control), states specific similarities AND differences, and makes an argument — for example, that fascism and communism were ideological opposites yet adopted strikingly similar totalitarian methods.

Totalitarian states were made possible by the tools of industrial modernity: mass propaganda through new media like radio and film, bureaucratic organization, the mobilization techniques pioneered in WWI's total war, and the modern state's expanded reach into citizens' lives.

Nazism's genocidal racism drew on the scientific racism and social Darwinism that nineteenth-century imperialism had normalized, showing a continuity between the ideologies of the age of imperialism and the atrocities of the twentieth century.

The interwar period is essentially the causes of World War II: a vengeful, rearming Germany, an expansionist Japan, a feeble League of Nations, and democracies too exhausted and distracted by economic crisis to stop the gathering storm.
